biggestGap: The one-square capture WALKS now, and on a slow renderer it is still not reliably DRAWN walking. `phase()` sizes every beat as `max(seconds, framePeriod * 2)`, but `framePeriod` is an EMA fed by `tune()` on the frames that came BEFORE the move — and the move itself flips `budget()` into its `moving` branch, which turns the shadow map on for every frame and the planar reflection from every 24th frame to every 3rd. The frames a walk is drawn in are structurally the most expensive frames the app ever draws, and the estimate that decides how long the walk lasts is taken from the cheapest. Measured, one-square Rxa2 through the canvas: the four idle frames before the click ran 0.017-0.050 s, the EMA nevertheless read 1.672 s, `phase` handed walkTo 3.344 s — and the very next frame, the first `moving` one, took 3.550 s. The whole approach expired inside it: ZERO rendered frames between a1 and the station, and a gap of 1.903 m at strike:call and the bit-identical 1.903 m at SHATTER. That is round 7’s 2.222/2.222 signature at a new address. It is not rare: across six instrumented one-square captures at 0.31-2.46 fps the approach was drawn in three runs (3, 3 and 2 frames) and NOT AT ALL in three. Above it sits a hard ceiling: `framePeriod` is clamped to FRAME_MAX = 2.5 s, so `phase` can never exceed 5.0 s, while the throttled run measured single frames of 3.784 s and 13.823 s — beyond about 2.5 s per frame no beat in the game can be drawn, by construction. And `driveSequences` cannot save it: its one-step-per-frame rule and its rebase protect the ORDER of the beats, but a walk is a single step whose pose is a continuous function of realTime, so nothing rebases a leg that one frame swallowed whole. The seven-square capture is fine for the same reason the one-square one is not — `walkSeconds` gives it 6.54 s, longer than any frame, and 8 of its frames showed the rook in motion.
critiqueDetail:
THE GUARANTEE HOLDS, UNCHANGED. king-surrender --t=2.8 is md5 45ebe28f78b6837bb2816b5fcccbe9ab at 2,264,723 bytes, the hash of rounds 3-7. wide-establishing --t=3 captured twice is cmp-clean byte-identical, md5 f64e1f7eee0c9fa66f15630a3334c5f8 at 2,630,788 bytes. verify-mate is 3/3 with legalReplies=0 on wreckage, strike and scholar. This was a read-only critique; nothing in the tree was touched. Note the two senses of the word: the frozen RENDER capture is unchanged, and that is the guarantee. The CHESS capture is not unchanged, and that is the round.

Q2 - THE ONE-SQUARE CAPTURE NOW WALKS, AND IT IS THE FIRST TIME IT HAS. Forced Rxa2 from 4k3/8/8/8/8/8/r7/R3K3, clicked through the real canvas on the production build, with walkTo / strike / destruction.shatter wrapped and timestamped and every piece sampled inside a wrapped lighting.render() — the last call of main.ts’s interactive frame, so a sample IS what was rasterised. walkTo WAS called, every run, before every strike. It goes to (0.591, 0.375): 43 degrees off the straight line, 0.695 squares = 1.634 m of ground, against the 0.14 squares that used to be dropped as negligible. planMove has no early-out left; standoffStation is the only source of a station and it is bounded below by MIN_APPROACH. Diagonal dxe5 walks 0.699 sq = 1.643 m to (3.669, 3.206). The knight walks its L: f3 -> f5 (the elbow, orthogonally adjacent) -> a closing 0.905 sq run to (4.625, 4.591), 2.633 squares in all. All three swing from beside the victim and not from their own square.

AND THE GAP NOW CLOSES ACROSS THE BLOW, WHICH IS THE NUMBER THAT MATTERS. Orthogonal Rxa2 at 0.89 fps: 2.269 m standing on a1, 1.903 m at strike:call, 1.624 m at SHATTER. Diagonal dxe5: 2.035 m at strike:call, 1.805 m at SHATTER. Knight Nxe5: 1.950 m at strike:call, 1.671 m at SHATTER. Round 7 measured 2.222 m and the identical 2.222 m. In every run the victim was drawn WHOLE, present in the frame table, in the last rendered frame before the shatter, with the attacker already at its station — strike:CONTACT carries vicDestroyed=false in all three, so the blow lands on a living man.

BUT ON A SLOW RENDERER THE WALK IS STILL NOT GUARANTEED TO REACH THE SCREEN. Six instrumented one-square captures, 0.31 to 2.46 fps: frames drawn strictly between origin and station were 3 (0.89 fps), 3 (0.84), 2 (0.82), and ZERO in three others (0.86 fps, 2.46 fps, 0.31 fps). In the zero runs the gap at strike:call and the gap at SHATTER are bit-identical — 1.903 and 1.903 — because the lunge fell between rasters too. The cause is measured in the gap above and it is a budgeting mistake, not a clock mistake. Under the 6x CPU throttle at 1280x800 the player’s first drawn frame after the click already has the rook standing at the station: a1 -> nothing for 5.6 s -> beside the victim. That is a teleport to the right place at the right time, which is better than round 7’s teleport to the wrong place at the wrong time, but it is not an approach.

Q3 - SPEED IS FIXED, AND THE FIX IS IN THE RIGHT PLACE. motion.ts now takes the caller’s `seconds` as a FLOOR only — `pdur = Math.max(dur, walkSeconds(dist))` — so choreography’s CHARGE_MAX clamp can no longer make a long move a fast one. walkSeconds prices metres at a cruise that FALLS with distance, 2.50 m/s down to 2.20 m/s over 12 m. Evaluated on the shipped curve at 20,000 samples per traverse: one square (2.35 m) is 0.946 s, mean 2.484 m/s, peak 4.477; seven squares (16.45 m) is 7.477 s, mean 2.200 m/s, peak 3.966. The long move is SLOWER, which is what was asked. Peak is 4.50 m/s — 16.2 km/h — against round 7’s 19.93 m/s / 71.7 km/h, a 4.4x reduction. GRIND is 0.28, so the peak-to-trough ripple inside a traverse is exactly 1.778x everywhere (it was 3.17x), and because the cruise law holds the shove rate near 3.5-4.6 Hz the cycle is now 13.1-17.1 frames at 60 fps instead of 4.0. Ease-in and ease-out are intact: v(0+) and v(end-) are ~3e-11 m/s.
  One wrinkle, reported because it is real: mean speed is not monotonic. MAX_TRAVEL caps a traverse at 9.4 s, which binds past 20.68 m = 8.80 squares, so the a1-h8 diagonal (23.26 m) runs at 2.475 m/s — 12.5% FASTER than the seven-square rook at 2.200. It stays under the one-square 2.484, so the file’s own claim that nothing beats the one-square cruise survives, by 9 mm/s. And the new law is expensive in time: a quiet rook a1-a8 is now 7.48 s of walking and a seven-square capture is about 8.8 s end to end, against the 3.31 s the previous plan priced. Nobody has looked at that yet.

Q4 - ONE CLOCK, AND IT IS world.realTime. interactive.ts’s update signature is `update(_t, realT)` — the scene-time argument is discarded. Every deadline, every sequence, every marker and `realNow` are realT. The only surviving mention of world.time in the file is inside `tune()`, which computes sceneRate purely to rescale the flare decay and shake it hands to lighting and camera — somebody else’s clocks — and schedules nothing. pieces/index.ts picks the same clock for the curves: `clock = () => playMode ? world.realTime : world.time` and `motion.update(playMode ? world.realTime : t)`. So beats and motion are on one clock in play. Under capture both are world.time and world.realTime is defined equal to it, which is why the md5 did not move. The 23.1-second dead hold between arriving and swinging that round 7 measured is gone: at 0.89 fps the arrive-to-swing hold is now 3.98 s and at 0.31 fps it is 13.9 s, both of which are frame periods rather than clock skew.
  THROTTLED HARD — 6x CPU throttle, 1280x800, plus a 120 ms busy loop pinned to the end of every frame — the page ran at 0.31 fps with a 13.823 s worst frame. Ordering survived it perfectly: walkTo called, station reached, victim whole and present for three consecutive drawn frames with the attacker beside it, then debris. The APPROACH did not survive it: zero frames in motion, 1.903 m at strike:call and 1.903 m at SHATTER. The step-in leg afterwards WAS drawn, three frames of it, because driveSequences scheduled it from a fresh clock reading rather than from the click.

Q5 - EIGHT MOVES CLICKED THROUGH THE CANVAS, THREE OF THEM CAPTURES, EVERY POSITION LEGAL. From the Italian r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N2N2/PPPP1PPP/R1BQK2R: Nxe5, Bxf7+, Rb1, Ra1, Rb1, Nxe4, Qe2, Ra1 — every one picked from the legal list, projected to screen coordinates through the app’s own live camera and clicked on the canvas, all eight accepted. The engine answered all eight: Nxe5, Nxf7, O-O, Qe7, Nxe4, Qxe4+, Qxg2, Qxh1+. Sixteen plies, eight captures in total, castling included. Every consecutive FEN pair was replayed through a FRESH engine bundled straight out of src/chess: 15/15 transitions reachable by a legal move, zero illegal, zero page errors, zero console errors. One transition needed two plies to match because the poller caught the engine’s reply inside a single read — a harness artefact, and the two-ply path was itself legal.

STILL OPEN FROM ROUND 7. clearBoard() in game/index.ts still only sets p.group.visible = false and never removes the instance from pieces/index.ts’s `live` array, so pieces.all() keeps returning every man from every staged position — my own frame sampler had to filter on group.visible to avoid tracking invisible pieces.

history.gap: none — 3/3 demo lines verified as real checkmate with zero legal replies

The play camera crops White's own back rank off the bottom of the frame — all eight rank-1 square centres sit 20-23 px below the canvas edge, leaving a 22-28 px sliver, so clicking where your own knight or king appears to be does nothing. Deterministic at every window size, and it hits on move 2.

You cannot tell what any piece is by looking at it. Every piece is the same pale armoured figure from behind and only height separates the types: rook 119.2 px, knight 132.2 px, bishop 141.1 px on screen — 13.0 px and 8.8 px apart, 7-11 percent of their own height, with no colour, crest or marking to help. It survives at full capture resolution, so it is not the software renderer. I picked all nine of my moves by reading the FEN out of the JS console; and since the HUD never prints state.lastMove, you also cannot tell what the engine just played.

The 32 carved pieces. They are 354,599 of the 404,665 triangles the phone submits every frame (87.6%), 56 of its 117 draw calls, and 1,065 ms of a 1,919 ms frame (55%) — measured by hiding exactly those 32 groups at a fixed 800x370 buffer and timing with a readPixels fence: 1,919 -> 854 ms, 117 -> 61 calls, 404,665 -> 50,066 triangles. The board, which this round rebuilt, is now 5 calls, 11,746 triangles and 296 ms; the chamber is 34 calls and 420 ms. src/pieces is the one module the round did not open. Every figure is uniquely carved, so nothing is instanced or merged; there is one body mesh plus one arm mesh per piece, no LOD of any kind, and a pawn 30 m away at the top of the frame carries the same ~11,000 triangles as the king a metre from the lens. 64 carved geometries are resident for the 32 men actually on the board.

The stone fragment shader on the 32 pieces. With geometry, draw calls (93), triangles (139,298) and screen coverage all held EXACTLY constant and only the piece material swapped, the frame is: shipped stone 1,717 ms / MeshStandard 1,317 / MeshLambert 1,083 / MeshBasic unlit 950 / pieces hidden 850. So of the 867 ms the pieces cost, rasterising them unlit is 100 ms (11%), lighting them over the 21 punctual lights is 133-367 ms, and the custom stone GLSL is ~400 ms ON TOP of PBR and ~767 ms over unlit — 45% of the whole frame, the single largest item left. The frame is fragment-bound and still is: through the app's own path at 0.116 / 0.189 / 0.314 Mpx it costs 850 / 1,217 / 1,767 ms, i.e. ~317 ms fixed plus 4,610 ms per megapixel, against round 4's 4,780 ms/Mpx. Cutting piece triangles 2.90x did not move that slope, because triangles were never what the slope was made of.

You cannot tell what any man on the board is. The top-down play camera that fixed the occlusion spent the one cue that was left. Projecting up to 900 vertices per mesh through the live camera at 1920x804, White's back rank draws: rook 98.8x85.5 px, knight 76.3x90.4, bishop 73.0x80.6, queen 67.4x79.9, king 71.2x86.0, pawn 80.1x76.5 — against world heights of 3.07 / 3.20 / 3.55 / 4.14 / 4.56 / 2.57 m. The ordering is not compressed, it is INVERTED: a 2.57 m pawn draws 80.1 px wide and the 4.14 m queen 67.4; the 3.20 m knight draws 90.4 px tall and the 4.56 m king 86.0. At 80 degrees of declination almost nothing of a man's height reaches the screen, so what is left is a plan-view footprint that is the same chamfered hexagon for all six types, and apparent size is set by WHERE a piece stands, not what it is. The image test says the same thing without reference to geometry: crop the eight men of rank 1 at 80x80 from refs/renders/play-critic.png, normalise each to zero mean and unit variance so exposure cannot fake a difference, and take mean absolute difference. Two men of the SAME type average 0.945 apart (RR 1.138, NN 0.875, BB 0.823) while two of DIFFERENT types average 0.819 — LESS. King against bishop is 0.533, the most similar pair on the rank; every different-type pair on the board is closer than the two rooks are to each other. The 20-px SVG glyph in the HUD tray reads instantly as a queen, a bishop, a knight. The 76-px carved model on the board does not. Nothing else on screen closes the gap: there are no rank/file coordinates anywhere (the Record panel prints 'Nxc2' and nothing tells you where c2 is), and interactive.ts never marks the engine's from/to squares — aff.setSelection / setDestinations / setCheck are the only board marks, and all three fire only for YOUR move.

Worse, the travel is now SHORTER than a frame: in dxe5 the pawn's walkTo(3.392,3.392) was ordered at wall 0.030 and its 0.40 s + 0.42 s settle had both expired by the next frame 3.066 s later, so not one frame of approach was ever rasterised. The pawn is drawn at (2.978,3.029) — d4 — in EVERY frame up to and including the one in which the victim shattered 3.312 m (1.409 squares) away, and appears on e5 only 7.08 real s AFTER the destruction. The engine's own reply in the same run is the player's original sentence verbatim: black-rook-07-74 struck white-rook-00-70 from (0.032,7.014) with a gap of 16.502 m — a8 to a1, seven squares — and the white rook shattered in that frame with its killer still standing on the far rank. Under it sits a frame-rate-INDEPENDENT residue: STANDOFF is 0.86 and NEGLIGIBLE is 0.15, so an orthogonally adjacent capture needs 1.00-0.86 = 0.14 squares of approach, misses the threshold by 0.01 square (2.4 cm), and planMove returns approach=[] with station = the attacker's own square. Measured: Rxa2 logged no walkTo before the strike, a gap of 2.222 m at strike:call and the identical 2.222 m at SHATTER. That one is what the code does at 60 fps too.
